screens.title: Storage Components of an Oracle Database
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will map the disk files and the logical storage units that make an Oracle database real. You will learn the purpose of data files, redo logs, control files, parameter files, and the password file. We will also build a clear mental model of database blocks, extents, segments, and tablespaces, and how those logical layers sit inside physical data files. This matters because backups, recovery, and performance are all rooted in these structures. For example, knowing that each data file belongs to a single tablespace helps you plan where to place files on storage arrays. You will also see why redo logs and control files are critical to recover committed transactions after a crash, and why multiplexing and disk separation are common best practices. As you go through the lesson, think about a database you manage and where its files live. That concrete mapping will make recovery plans and capacity planning practical and reliable. At the end, you'll be able to explain the storage hierarchy and list the files you must protect to avoid data loss.

screens.title: Learning Objectives

First, you will be able to identify and describe key physical files — data files, redo logs, control files, parameter files, and the password file. For each objective we include a short mnemonic or visual cue to help memory. As you practice, verify competency by listing files and interpreting a small set of S Q L*Plus outputs. These tasks replicate common DBA checks and prepare you to avoid single points of failure.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Checks

screens.title: Physical Storage: Data Files
screens.narratorSegment: Data files are the place where Oracle writes the actual rows, index entries, and metadata blocks. They are simple operating system files with an internal structure made of database blocks. Each data file belongs to exactly one tablespace. That single-membership rule means a tablespace is a logical container composed of one or more files. When you create a table, Oracle allocates blocks inside the data files of the tablespace that owns the table. The size and number of data files determine how much data that tablespace can hold. An example: if a tablespace uses two 10 gigabyte data files, the total capacity is the sum of those files. A common misconception is to treat tablespaces like files; they are logical constructs and can span multiple files. Another practical point is that blocks are the smallest input and output unit and are defined by DB_BLOCK_SIZE at creation time. Because the block size cannot change later, you must plan it at database creation. For daily administration, you will list data files, check their status, and note size and tablespace membership. The key takeaway is: protect and monitor data files as the primary containers of persisted data, and remember they are the physical anchors for logical tablespaces and segments.

keyIdea.text: Data files store blocks for tables and indexes; each file belongs to a single tablespace and sets physical capacity.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Data Files
Core Concept
Data Files (.dbf)
Files that store tables, indexes, and metadata blocks. They define tablespace capacity.
Database blocks inside data files are the smallest I/O unit defined by DB_BLOCK_SIZE at creation.
Each data file belongs to one tablespace. The tablespace may have multiple files.
Segment allocations use extents, which are contiguous blocks inside these files.
Key Takeaway
Treat data files as physical containers for tablespaces and monitor their size and status closely.
Visual explanation
Tablespace A
datafile_a01.dbf
16 GB
Tablespace A
datafile_a02.dbf
8 GB
Tablespace B
datafile_b01.dbf
32 GB
Concrete example
A table in Tablespace A will have its blocks stored inside datafile_a01 or a02. The tablespace capacity is the sum of those files.
Common mistake
Assuming a tablespace equals a single file. In reality it can span multiple files across disks.

screens.title: Online Redo Logs and Recovery
screens.narratorSegment: Online redo log files record every change to the database in sequence and are essential for recovering after an instance crash. The Log Writer process writes redo records to the current online log group and cycles through groups as they fill. Oracle requires a minimum of two log groups to support this cyclical pattern. When ARCHIVELOG mode is enabled, the ARCH process copies filled redo members to archived redo logs before they are reused. That enables point-in-time recovery by applying archived logs to backups. Multiplexing redo log members—placing identical log members on different physical disks—protects against media failure. A common error is keeping all members on the same drive; if that drive fails, you may lose required redo and be unable to recover committed transactions. Consider an example: if a database commits transactions and a crash occurs before the datafile changes are written, the redo contains those changes. Without the redo files you cannot guarantee those commits. The correct practice is to have multiple members per group on separate disks and ensure archival and backups are in place. Reflect: how would you verify that redo groups are multiplexed on your system?

keyIdea.title: Redo log role
keyIdea.text: Redo logs chronicle changes for recovery; multiplex and archive them to avoid losing committed transactions.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Redo Logs
Process Flow
Online Redo Log Cycle
Log writer writes sequentially to a group. When full, it switches to the next group. Archived copies allow point-in-time recovery.
1
LGWR writes redo entries to the current group as transactions commit.
2
When the group fills, LGWR switches to the next group and the filled files become candidates for archival.
3
ARCH copies filled members to archive logs if ARCHIVELOG mode is enabled.
Concrete example
Two groups, each with two members on separate disks, ensure a single disk failure won't lose an entire group.
Common mistake
Placing all redo members on one array creates a single point of failure despite having multiple members.
Quick checks
Use the V$LOGFILE and V$LOG views to list groups and members and confirm multiplexing and sizes.
Always keep at least two groups. Multiplex each member on different disks when possible.
If ARCHIVELOG is required for your recovery SLA, ensure archive destinations are healthy and monitored.
Remember: losing all redo logs prevents opening the database without restoring from backups and archives, risking data loss.

screens.title: Control Files and Multiplexing
screens.narratorSegment: Control files are small binary files that hold metadata required to open and manage the database. They include the database name, the list and locations of data files and online redo logs, the current log sequence, checkpoint information, and backup metadata. Because the control file lists where every critical file lives, losing all copies prevents the database from opening without manual reconstruction or a backup. For that reason Oracle recommends multiplexing control files—keeping identical control files on different disks. Imagine a system with three control file copies across two storage arrays. If one disk fails, the database still has the other copies and can continue. A typical misconception is to assume control files are small and unimportant to back up; they are essential. If a control file is accidentally deleted while the database is running, the instance may continue until shutdown, but restart will fail unless you restore the missing copy. The practical steps for recovery are to copy an existing valid control file back to the missing location and restart. This is why regular backups and configuration of multiple control files matter for availability and recoverability.

keyIdea.text: Control files store the database map and must be multiplexed; losing all copies prevents opening the database.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Control Files
Core Concept
Control Files (.ctl)
Binary files that record database structure and state needed to open and recover the database.
They record datafile and redo log locations, the current log sequence, and checkpoint info.
Multiplexing across different disks reduces risk of a single disk failure making the database unparsable.
If all control files are lost, manual reconstruction or a backup copy is required to open the database.
Common mistake
Storing all control files on the same physical disk or array and treating them as non-critical duplicates.
Multiplexing example
A database with three control file locations on separate mount points is resilient to a single disk failure.
/u01/oradata/db/ctrl01.ctl
/u02/oradata/db/ctrl02.ctl
/u03/oradata/db/ctrl03.ctl
Concrete recovery step
If one copy is deleted, shut down if needed, copy a valid copy to the missing path with the same name, and restart the database.
Pro tip
Include control files in your backup plan and test restore steps to ensure you can recover if a copy is lost.

screens.title: PFILE vs SPFILE
screens.narratorSegment: Oracle supports two parameter file formats. The PFILE is a plain text initialization file you can edit manually. If you change parameters in a PFILE you must restart the database for the changes to take effect. The SPFILE is a binary server parameter file that persists changes made with ALTER SYSTEM when SCOPE is SPFILE or BOTH. Because SPFILE records persistent changes and supports dynamic tuning without manual file edits, it is the recommended approach in modern environments. An example: increasing a memory parameter with ALTER SYSTEM SET... SCOPE=SPFILE ensures the new value survives a restart. A common misconception is that SPFILE prevents any mistakes; it does not. Mistakes committed to an SPFILE still persist until you change them or restore a previous SPFILE. For emergency recoveries, having a PFILE available as a fallback can be helpful. Administrators often keep a known-good PFILE as an emergency manual startup option. The key contrast to remember: PFILE is editable text and requires restart; SPFILE is binary and persistent for dynamic changes. PFILE vs SPFILE means pfile is editable text and needs restart; spfile is binary, persists dynamic changes, and is the recommended production choice.. In practical terms, text parameter file versus binary server parameter file and when to use each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › PFILE vs SPFILE
PFILE and SPFILE
A side-by-side comparison of text and binary initialization files and their operational implications.
PFILE (text)
Plain text file. Editable with a text editor. Changes require a restart to take effect.
Use case: emergency manual edits and known-good startup files.
Common misconception
That manual edits are always safer. Manual edits can introduce typos; validate before startup.
SPFILE (binary)
Binary, persistent file updated by ALTER SYSTEM with SCOPE=SPFILE or BOTH. Recommended for production.
Use case: dynamic tuning and persistent configuration changes.
Pro tip
Keep a PFILE backup of a known-good SPFILE as a recovery option if you need to rebuild the binary file.
Key Takeaway

Use SPFILE for persistent dynamic changes. Keep a PFILE as a resilient fallback for manual startup when necessary.

screens.title: Password File (orapwd) and Administrative Access
screens.narratorSegment: The password file, typically created with the orapwd utility, stores encrypted credentials that allow administrative users to connect with SYSDBA or SYSOPER privileges even when the database is not open. This capability is essential for emergency operations such as instance startup, shutdown, or recovery tasks that require privileged connections before the database is mounted or opened. Security of the password file is critical because it grants powerful privileges when present. A common error is to leave the password file world-readable or to reuse weak passwords, which could allow unauthorized administrative access. The password file is separate from the database user table and should be managed with care. In some environments, administrators maintain a single password file copy on a secure location and control access through operating system permissions. A concrete example: when a server boots and you need to mount the database for recovery, you can connect as SYS using the password file without the database being open. The takeaway is to secure, back up, and control access to the password file as part of your operational and compliance procedures.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Password File
Password File (orapwd)
Encrypted file that enables SYSDBA and SYSOPER connections when the database is not open.
Purpose
Allow privileged remote connections prior to database open.
Security
Protect with strict OS permissions; loss or exposure risks administrative control.
Practical tip
Keep a backup copy and ensure only authorized operators can read or write it.
Concrete example
Use orapwd to create a file and verify that SYS connections at mount time succeed without opening the database.
Common mistake
Leaving the password file accessible to more than the DBA group increases risk of unauthorized SYS access.

screens.title: Logical Storage: Blocks, Extents, Segments, Tablespaces
screens.narratorSegment: Oracle arranges stored data with a clear hierarchy that begins at the database block and rises to tablespaces. The database block is the smallest unit of input and output; reads and writes happen at the block level. Extents are contiguous groups of blocks allocated to a segment when it needs space. A segment is a collection of extents allocated for a logical object such as a table or an index. Finally, a tablespace groups related segments and is composed of one or more data files. This layered arrangement provides flexibility. For instance, you can add or move data files belonging to a tablespace without changing the logical definition of the tables stored inside. A concrete example: when a table grows, Oracle will allocate a new extent inside one of the tablespace's files to hold the new blocks. A frequent misconception is to equate segments with files; segments may span multiple files through extents. The practical significance is that tablespace and extent allocation affect fragmentation, performance, and space management. Understanding this hierarchy helps you predict storage growth and plan tablespace layout to reduce input and output hotspots and make backups more manageable.

keyIdea.title: Storage hierarchy
keyIdea.text: Blocks form extents, extents form segments, and segments are grouped in tablespaces that map to data files.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Logical Hierarchy
Blocks → Extents → Segments → Tablespaces
A hierarchical view that explains how logical objects map into physical space.
Block
Smallest I/O unit defined by DB_BLOCK_SIZE.
Extent
Contiguous blocks allocated to a segment.
Segment
Set of extents for a table, index, or rollback segment.
Tablespace
Logical container composed of one or more data files.
Concrete example
A growing table receives new extents in the tablespace's data files. That growth is visible as increased file usage on disk.
Misconception
Segments are not the same as files; they may span many files via extents inside a tablespace.

screens.title: Mapping Logical Structures to Physical Files
screens.narratorSegment: Mapping logical structures to physical files is the practical skill that connects planning to operations. A tablespace groups segments and is implemented as one or more data files on disk. When a table needs space, Oracle allocates extents from those files, which are composed of contiguous blocks. This mapping influences backup scope, input and output distribution, and the ability to move or resize storage. For example, if you place hot tables in a single tablespace whose files are all on the same disk array, input and output contention may occur; splitting those tables across tablespaces with files on different disks can balance load. Another practical concern is moving a tablespace's files to a new disk: you can add new data files on the target disk and then perform data movement operations that populate the new files, finally dropping the old ones. A common misstep is not checking file statuses and sizes before an operation; always confirm file online status and free space in extents. The key operational insight is that logical design decisions have direct impacts on physical storage and performance, so plan tablespaces deliberately and monitor their file mappings.

keyIdea.title: Mapping insight
keyIdea.text: Tablespaces are logical groups composed of data files; placement of those files determines capacity, I/O distribution, and recovery scopes.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Logical → Physical
Mapping Logical Structures to Files
Practical implications for placement, performance, and recovery.
Scenario
Tablespace containing a hot table with files on a single array leads to I/O contention.
Solution: create a new tablespace with files on a different disk and move the table.
Concrete example
Add datafile on target disk, migrate data to the new tablespace or use transportable tablespace techniques to rebalance I/O.
Operational checks
Verify file STATUS, SIZE, and TABLESPACE membership using DBA_DATA_FILES. Confirm free space and extent fragmentation before moves.
Common mistake
Assuming moving files is only a filesystem task. Logical mappings and Oracle metadata must be handled correctly to avoid inconsistencies.
Key Takeaway

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Inspecting Files
SQL*Plus File Inspection
Run these queries to list critical files and map them to tablespaces.
-- 1. List data files and tablespaces
SELECT FILE_NAME, TABLESPACE_NAME, BYTES/1024/1024 AS SIZE_MB, STATUS
FROM DBA_DATA_FILES
-- 2. List online redo log groups and members
SELECT GROUP#, STATUS, MEMBER, BYTES/1024/1024 AS SIZE_MB
FROM V$LOGFILE
-- 3. List control files
SELECT NAME FROM V$CONTROLFILE
-- 4. Tablespace summary
SELECT TABLESPACE_NAME, STATUS, CONTENTS, LOGGING FROM DBA_TABLESPACES
Concrete interpretation
If V$LOGFILE shows members on different mount points, multiplexing is configured. If all members are under the same mount, plan to relocate copies.
Scenario exercise
You inherit a system. Run these queries, then answer: which tablespace files are on a single disk, which redo groups lack multiple members, and where are control files located?
Common mistake
Assuming default file placement is safe without checking actual mount points and array layouts. Always confirm physical locations.
Key Takeaway

These queries are the fastest way to build an accurate map of where your logical structures are stored and whether redundancy is in place.

screens.title: Best Practices: Multiplexing and Disk Separation
screens.narratorSegment: Two practical best practices dominate safe storage design: multiplex critical files and separate file types across disks or arrays. Multiplexing means keeping identical copies of control files and redo log members on distinct physical devices. This protects you from media failure of a single disk. Separating file types—data files on one set of arrays, redo logs on another, and control files on separate disks—reduces input and output contention and ensures that a failure in one pool does not remove multiple file types at once. For example, placing redo logs on dedicated low-latency devices improves write performance because LGWR writes sequentially. A common mistaken approach is to prioritize convenience and consolidate all files on a single high-capacity array. That creates a single point of failure and often increases latency for critical writes. Practically, verify multiplexing with V$LOGFILE, confirm control files in multiple paths, and plan tablespace placement according to workload. Regular backups and testing of recovery procedures complete the approach. Ask yourself: if a disk fails, can you restart and recover without losing committed work? If not, adjust multiplexing and file placement until the answer is yes.

Multiplexing and Disk Separation
Practical layout rules to reduce risk and improve performance.
Redo logs
Place members on multiple disks and prefer dedicated low-latency devices for sequential writes.
Control files
Multiplex control files on separate physical devices to avoid an unrecoverable restart.
Data files
Distribute large or hot tablespaces across arrays to reduce I/O hotspots and allow targeted backups.

Use three control file copies on three mount points, redo members on two arrays, and place heavy OLTP tablespaces on dedicated spindles or LUNs.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will map the disk files and the logical storage units that make an Oracle database real. You will learn the purpose of data files, redo logs, control files, parameter files, and the password file. We will also build a clear mental model of database blocks, extents, segments, and tablespaces, and how those logical layers sit inside physical data files. This matters because backups, recovery, and performance are all rooted in these structures. For example, knowing that each data file belongs to a single tablespace helps you plan where to place files on storage arrays. You will also see why redo logs and control files are critical to recover committed transactions after a crash, and why multiplexing and disk separation are common best practices. As you go through the lesson, think about a database you manage and where its files live. That concrete mapping will make recovery plans and capacity planning practical and reliable. At the end, you'll be able to explain the storage hierarchy and list the files you must protect to avoid data loss.

These objectives will guide your attention as you study storage components. First, you will be able to identify and describe key physical files — data files, redo logs, control files, parameter files, and the password file. That means you can locate their paths and explain the role each plays in normal operations and recovery. Second, you will learn the logical hierarchy from blocks up to tablespaces, so you can explain how a table's data lives inside blocks and extents that belong to a segment within a tablespace. Third, you will practice mapping logical structures to physical files. This is crucial when you must plan capacity, move files, or interpret backup output. Finally, you will recognize the role of control files and redo logs in recovery and the need to multiplex and separate them. For each objective we include a short mnemonic or visual cue to help memory. As you practice, verify competency by listing files and interpreting a small set of S Q L*Plus outputs. These tasks replicate common DBA checks and prepare you to avoid single points of failure.

This second objectives card is task-focused. You will practice specific checks that reveal how the database is laid out and whether your recovery posture is correct. Learn to run the S Q L*Plus queries that list data files, redo log members, and control files, and to read their results meaningfully. For example, a data file marked offline or read-only has different implications than one that is online but small. You will also learn to check whether the instance uses an SPFILE or PFILE, and why SPFILE is recommended when you want dynamic parameter changes to persist. Finally, develop the habit of confirming multiplexed control files and redo log members on separate disks. A common misconception is that backup alone protects you; in practice, the correct placement and copies of redo and control files are required for many recovery scenarios. These practical skills let you answer the question: can I restart and recover this database if a disk fails?

Data files are the place where Oracle writes the actual rows, index entries, and metadata blocks. They are simple operating system files with an internal structure made of database blocks. Each data file belongs to exactly one tablespace. That single-membership rule means a tablespace is a logical container composed of one or more files. When you create a table, Oracle allocates blocks inside the data files of the tablespace that owns the table. The size and number of data files determine how much data that tablespace can hold. An example: if a tablespace uses two 10 gigabyte data files, the total capacity is the sum of those files. A common misconception is to treat tablespaces like files; they are logical constructs and can span multiple files. Another practical point is that blocks are the smallest input and output unit and are defined by DB_BLOCK_SIZE at creation time. Because the block size cannot change later, you must plan it at database creation. For daily administration, you will list data files, check their status, and note size and tablespace membership. The key takeaway is: protect and monitor data files as the primary containers of persisted data, and remember they are the physical anchors for logical tablespaces and segments.

Online redo log files record every change to the database in sequence and are essential for recovering after an instance crash. The Log Writer process writes redo records to the current online log group and cycles through groups as they fill. Oracle requires a minimum of two log groups to support this cyclical pattern. When ARCHIVELOG mode is enabled, the ARCH process copies filled redo members to archived redo logs before they are reused. That enables point-in-time recovery by applying archived logs to backups. Multiplexing redo log members—placing identical log members on different physical disks—protects against media failure. A common error is keeping all members on the same drive; if that drive fails, you may lose required redo and be unable to recover committed transactions. Consider an example: if a database commits transactions and a crash occurs before the datafile changes are written, the redo contains those changes. Without the redo files you cannot guarantee those commits. The correct practice is to have multiple members per group on separate disks and ensure archival and backups are in place. Reflect: how would you verify that redo groups are multiplexed on your system?

Control files are small binary files that hold metadata required to open and manage the database. They include the database name, the list and locations of data files and online redo logs, the current log sequence, checkpoint information, and backup metadata. Because the control file lists where every critical file lives, losing all copies prevents the database from opening without manual reconstruction or a backup. For that reason Oracle recommends multiplexing control files—keeping identical control files on different disks. Imagine a system with three control file copies across two storage arrays. If one disk fails, the database still has the other copies and can continue. A typical misconception is to assume control files are small and unimportant to back up; they are essential. If a control file is accidentally deleted while the database is running, the instance may continue until shutdown, but restart will fail unless you restore the missing copy. The practical steps for recovery are to copy an existing valid control file back to the missing location and restart. This is why regular backups and configuration of multiple control files matter for availability and recoverability.

Oracle supports two parameter file formats. The PFILE is a plain text initialization file you can edit manually. If you change parameters in a PFILE you must restart the database for the changes to take effect. The SPFILE is a binary server parameter file that persists changes made with ALTER SYSTEM when SCOPE is SPFILE or BOTH. Because SPFILE records persistent changes and supports dynamic tuning without manual file edits, it is the recommended approach in modern environments. An example: increasing a memory parameter with ALTER SYSTEM SET... SCOPE=SPFILE ensures the new value survives a restart. A common misconception is that SPFILE prevents any mistakes; it does not. Mistakes committed to an SPFILE still persist until you change them or restore a previous SPFILE. For emergency recoveries, having a PFILE available as a fallback can be helpful. Administrators often keep a known-good PFILE as an emergency manual startup option. The key contrast to remember: PFILE is editable text and requires restart; SPFILE is binary and persistent for dynamic changes. PFILE vs SPFILE means pfile is editable text and needs restart; spfile is binary, persists dynamic changes, and is the recommended production choice.. In practical terms, text parameter file versus binary server parameter file and when to use each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The password file, typically created with the orapwd utility, stores encrypted credentials that allow administrative users to connect with SYSDBA or SYSOPER privileges even when the database is not open. This capability is essential for emergency operations such as instance startup, shutdown, or recovery tasks that require privileged connections before the database is mounted or opened. Security of the password file is critical because it grants powerful privileges when present. A common error is to leave the password file world-readable or to reuse weak passwords, which could allow unauthorized administrative access. The password file is separate from the database user table and should be managed with care. In some environments, administrators maintain a single password file copy on a secure location and control access through operating system permissions. A concrete example: when a server boots and you need to mount the database for recovery, you can connect as SYS using the password file without the database being open. The takeaway is to secure, back up, and control access to the password file as part of your operational and compliance procedures.

Oracle arranges stored data with a clear hierarchy that begins at the database block and rises to tablespaces. The database block is the smallest unit of input and output; reads and writes happen at the block level. Extents are contiguous groups of blocks allocated to a segment when it needs space. A segment is a collection of extents allocated for a logical object such as a table or an index. Finally, a tablespace groups related segments and is composed of one or more data files. This layered arrangement provides flexibility. For instance, you can add or move data files belonging to a tablespace without changing the logical definition of the tables stored inside. A concrete example: when a table grows, Oracle will allocate a new extent inside one of the tablespace's files to hold the new blocks. A frequent misconception is to equate segments with files; segments may span multiple files through extents. The practical significance is that tablespace and extent allocation affect fragmentation, performance, and space management. Understanding this hierarchy helps you predict storage growth and plan tablespace layout to reduce input and output hotspots and make backups more manageable.

Mapping logical structures to physical files is the practical skill that connects planning to operations. A tablespace groups segments and is implemented as one or more data files on disk. When a table needs space, Oracle allocates extents from those files, which are composed of contiguous blocks. This mapping influences backup scope, input and output distribution, and the ability to move or resize storage. For example, if you place hot tables in a single tablespace whose files are all on the same disk array, input and output contention may occur; splitting those tables across tablespaces with files on different disks can balance load. Another practical concern is moving a tablespace's files to a new disk: you can add new data files on the target disk and then perform data movement operations that populate the new files, finally dropping the old ones. A common misstep is not checking file statuses and sizes before an operation; always confirm file online status and free space in extents. The key operational insight is that logical design decisions have direct impacts on physical storage and performance, so plan tablespaces deliberately and monitor their file mappings.
